title: APRA now digging into $3.4bn Bathla blow-up
full_text:
The prudential regulator has waded into the crisis engulfing home builder Bathla Group to assess whether there are contagion risks from its $3.4bn crunch.
If Bathla collapses, it would drag down with it suppliers, staff, and lenders. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority has been reviewing the matter, which has largely been a private credit-funded story, amid concerns it could spread into more regulated parts of the financial system.
Bathla entered voluntary administration on August 24, and since then The Australian has learned APRA contacted a number of regulated institutions to determine their exposure. While no Australian banks were lenders to Bathla, beyond Commonwealth Bank which is owed $900,000 for the developer’s unpaid credit card bill, many are exposed to suppliers, customers, and staff.
MST Marquee senior analyst Brian Johnson warned in a note to clients recently the risks for the banking system sat with Bathla’s subcontractors. Many of these have gone unpaid for months and some are owed more than $10m. Many will have unsecured working capital facilities to fund their costs, or have pledged homes against loans.
Five lenders have backed administrator Teneo’s attempt to raise $5m to keep head office functioning and complete projects across Sydney’s western fringe.
Suppliers to these projects will likely see some of the funds they are owed, but many on the 45 projects Bathla had active prior to its collapse will see nothing.
National Australia Bank has the greatest exposure to the construction sector among the big four, with 1.4 per cent of its loan book tied up. This is followed by Westpac, with 1.1 per cent. Several major banks have also provided wholesale credit lines to lenders.
APRA has also tapped superannuation funds for information on their exposure to private credit lenders at last count owed in excess of $3.1bn. Among the biggest backers of Bathla are Centuria Bass, Credit Connect, PAG, Balmain, CVS Lane and Leda.
Several have frozen redemptions meaning their investors can’t reclaim their money.
On Thursday, NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the Minns government had assembled a working group to review the crisis. The NSW Labor government was not going to “come to the rescue of private credit”, he repeated, because those lenders “knew full well what they were getting themselves into”.
“We do consider it the job of Bathla’s creditors to step in and organise the future of the company,” he said.
His priority is people who put deposits down on Bathla properties. “They come first before the interest of bankers,” he said.
Several more lenders have appointed receivers over land sites controlled by the developer in recent days. Among these are Keyview Financial, RELI Capita, Driat, and Centaur Property.
More lenders are calling in receivers and following the lead of Ray White Capital, Balmain Group and Woodbridge Capital. Newpoint Advisory has been called in as receiver by smaller lenders. These include small positions held by real estate private credit and investment manager IDA, which is backed by a real estate fund managed by Macquarie Asset Management’s real estate division.
